items.prompt: What does formal authority come from?
choices: A long track record of giving sound advice to peers
A title that gives the right to decide or approve
Being well liked by most of the people in the group
items.explanation: Formal authority is attached to a position; it exists because of the role.

items.prompt: Which of these is an example of informal authority?
choices: A teammate whose judgment people seek before choosing
A manager assigning tasks to people reporting to them
A director signing the quarterly budget request
items.explanation: Informal authority is influence earned through trust, with no title behind it.

items.prompt: Dev manages nobody in the steering meeting. What can he still have?
choices: Approval rights inherited from his engineer title
Delegated voting power from the committee chair
Influence built on trust
items.explanation: With no decision role, trust and credibility are what is left.

items.prompt: Where does informal authority stop?
choices: At the edge of the person's own team
At the level of the person's direct manager, whatever their record
Nowhere in particular, since no box on a chart holds it
items.explanation: It is not tied to a position, so it can cross teams and reporting lines.

items.prompt: The power to approve a budget is called what?
choices: Informal authority, because it is exercised quietly
Formal authority, because it comes with the role
Reciprocal authority, because it is traded
items.explanation: The right to approve is granted by the title, which makes it formal.

items.prompt: Which statement about informal authority is true?
choices: It is earned through behavior rather than assigned
It is granted automatically at promotion time
It is listed in the written job description and reviewed yearly
items.explanation: Trust is built by what someone has actually done.

items.prompt: In the school story, the student wants the shorter trip but cannot vote. What do they hold?
choices: No formal authority, but some possible influence
Formal authority as a member of the school
The same decision power as the principal
items.explanation: Belonging to the group is not a decision role; influence is all that is available.

items.prompt: Which is the best short definition of informal authority?
choices: The right to approve decisions for a small group
Power that is written down but rarely used
Influence that does not come from a title
items.explanation: The defining feature is that it works without an official role.

items.prompt: Two engineers disagree about an approach. One is the team's manager. The other has no title, but the team was right to follow her advice on the last five calls. Which statement describes the situation best?
choices: Both hold formal authority, because both of them work on the same team and answer to one manager
Only the manager holds any real authority at all, because the engineer has no official role to point to
The manager holds formal authority, while the engineer holds informal authority built on her record
The engineer holds formal authority, because being right so many times in a row is what creates a title
items.explanation: The manager's power comes from the role; the engineer's comes from the record she built. Neither requires the other.
items.reference:
Formal authority

Comes from a title: assign, approve, say yes or no

Informal authority

Comes from trust and credibility, no title needed

Why: a title is not required to move a decision; trust and credibility do real work on their own.

items.prompt: After a reorganization, a respected engineer loses her title, but former colleagues still seek her opinion. What happened to her two kinds of authority?
choices: The formal kind went and the informal kind stayed, since it rested on trust
Both kinds were lost together, since informal authority cannot survive without a title behind it
The formal kind stayed and the informal kind faded away, as people's opinions usually do over time
Neither kind changed at all, since a reorganization only moves reporting lines around the chart
items.explanation: Informal authority was never attached to the position, so a title change does not remove it.

choices: A louder argument made in the meeting itself
An appeal to the most senior person around
The seniority that his job title implies
Trust and credibility with the people who hold the decision
items.explanation: With no formal lever, influence has to come from how much the deciders already trust his judgment.

items.prompt: A new manager has formal authority over a team but no history with them, and the team quietly ignores her suggestions. What does this show?
choices: Formal authority is meaningless in practice, so she should give up the title and start over
A title grants the right to decide but does not by itself earn trust
The team is breaking the rules, so they should be reprimanded by someone more senior
Informal authority can only be built by people who hold no title, so she must stay out of it
items.explanation: Formal authority is real, but being followed willingly depends on informal authority, which has to be earned.

items.prompt: Who is the nominal decision-maker?
choices: The person who talks the most in meetings
The person whose name is on the sign-off
The person who knows the topic in most detail
items.explanation: Nominal means by name: the official owner of the decision.

items.prompt: Who are the real decision-makers?
choices: The people with the longest tenure at the company
The people whose input the signer cannot comfortably overrule
The people who attend every single meeting held on the topic
items.explanation: Real power sits with whoever the signer actually defers to.

items.prompt: VP Farid signs whatever the four tech leads agree on. Who really decides?
choices: Farid, because the signature is his alone
Nobody, until the meeting has begun
The four tech leads
items.explanation: Farid's habit is to defer, so the leads' consensus is the real decision.

items.prompt: Which question finds the real decision-makers?
choices: Whose objection would actually stop this?
Who holds the most senior title in the room?
Who will speak first when the meeting opens?
items.explanation: The test is about who can block the outcome, not who is listed.

items.prompt: In the school story, who in practice decides the length of the trip?
choices: The student who wants the shorter trip
The four parent representatives
Whoever arrives at the meeting first
items.explanation: The principal signs, but follows the representatives' agreement.

items.prompt: What is the risk of convincing only the nominal decision-maker?
choices: The real decision may already have been made elsewhere
The signer may sign the paper before reading the whole proposal
The meeting may be scheduled too soon
items.explanation: Effort aimed at the wrong person does not move the outcome.

items.prompt: A decision-maker asks 'what do you all think?' before deciding. What does it suggest?
choices: They have already made up their mind
They want the meeting to finish quickly
They defer to the people they are asking
items.explanation: Asking first is a signal that the answer comes from those people.

items.prompt: Do the nominal and real maps always match?
choices: Yes; they are always the very same people
Yes; unless the company is very large
No; they often overlap but can differ
items.explanation: Titles show who signs; they do not show whose judgment counts.

items.prompt: A director asks three team leads for a recommendation and signs whatever they agree on, though he could technically overrule them. Who are the real decision-makers?
choices: The director, because his is the signature that is formally required
The three team leads, because the director follows their consensus
The team members, because the leads speak on their behalf in the room
Nobody, because a signature without a vote is not a real decision
items.explanation: Capacity to overrule is not the same as practice. The signer's behavior shows whose input counts.
items.reference:
🖋️ Nominal decision-maker: the name on the sign-off
🧭 Real decision-makers: whose input the signer cannot comfortably overrule
❓ Test: whose objection would actually stop it?

Why: arguing to the signer while the real decision was made elsewhere is a common, avoidable failure.

choices: The fact that she shares a title with the other three leads
How often she attends the committee's regular meetings
Whether she is on friendly terms with the other three
Past cases where her disagreement delayed or changed something Farid signed
items.explanation: The real map shows up in past outcomes, not in titles or attendance.

items.prompt: A proposal is blocked even though its owner agrees with it. A peer team's lead objected and the owner backed off. What does this reveal?
choices: The peer lead was a real decision-maker the org chart did not list
The owner lacked the nominal authority to approve anything without the peer's permission
The peer lead outranks the owner on the organization chart, so the owner had to give way
The objection was only a short delay and had no real effect on the final outcome
items.explanation: The decision followed the peer's objection, which is how the real map shows itself.

items.prompt: Dev can reach only one person before the meeting, and Farid defers to the leads' consensus. Which choice best fits the real map?
choices: Farid, because he is the one whose signature the decision needs
No one, so that every attendee hears the case at the same time
The most affected tech lead, since the leads' consensus is what Farid signs
The whole committee at once, using one identical email sent to every single member
items.explanation: Effort belongs where the decision is actually made, which here is the leads' consensus.

items.prompt: What is a coalition?
choices: People who attend the same meeting that you do
People who support your position before the decision moment
People who report to the same manager as you
items.explanation: A coalition is built in advance, not assembled on the day.

items.prompt: When is coalition-building most likely to work?
choices: Days or weeks before the meeting
During the meeting itself, in front of everyone
Right after the decision has been announced
items.explanation: Private time gives people room to reconsider.

items.prompt: Why is changing your mind in front of an audience hard?
choices: It can feel like losing face
The audience always prefers the first idea they heard
Meetings are too short for anyone to hear arguments
items.explanation: Social pressure makes a live change costly.

items.prompt: Dev raises his concern for the first time in the meeting. What usually happens?
choices: Everyone adopts his position on the spot
The signer cancels the meeting and asks Dev to start again
People default to the position they walked in with
items.explanation: A cold ask has no time to land.

items.prompt: What does a coalition built before the meeting change?
choices: The signer no longer attends the meeting
The signer hears a shared recommendation, not one lone objection
The meeting no longer needs to reach a decision
items.explanation: By the time Dev speaks, several people already agree.

items.prompt: Why talk to the most persuadable person first?
choices: They always have the highest title of the group
Their agreement helps the next conversation
They never ask any questions of their own
items.explanation: Each early agreement changes the frame for the next person.

items.prompt: Which setting best allows someone to reconsider?
choices: A packed room with the signer watching closely
A group chat that includes the whole company
A private one-on-one conversation
items.explanation: Less audience means less pressure.

items.prompt: How far ahead should the early conversations happen?
choices: Far enough ahead for people to think it over
Minutes before the meeting starts
Only after the vote is held
items.explanation: Reflection needs time.

items.prompt: Dev has twelve days. Which plan best uses the time?
choices: Prepare one excellent presentation and deliver it in the meeting
Send everyone the same long email on day eleven
Wait for objections in the meeting, then answer each
Talk privately to the decision-makers in turn, starting with the most persuadable
items.explanation: Early, ordered, private conversations are what the timing logic favors.
items.reference:
During the meetingBefore the meeting
Time to reconsiderNone, on the spotDays, in private
Social pressureHigh, audience watchingLow, one-on-one
Likely outcomePrior position holdsArrives already aligned

Why: people rarely change a position live, in front of others, without time to think.
items.learnMore:
Coalition timing and order

The same argument, made at two different times, has very different odds of changing anyone's mind. The order of conversations also compounds.

TimingWhat happens
During the meeting, coldPositions default; changing one live feels like losing face
Days before, one-on-oneRoom to reconsider and arrive aligned
Weeks before, in orderEarly converts help win over holdouts
items.reflection: Recall a time you changed your mind about something. Did it happen in front of others or in private, and why does that difference matter?

items.prompt: Two colleagues lean toward Dev's view after private talks. Why does mentioning this honestly to a third colleague help?
choices: It lets Dev pressure the third person into agreeing before she has had time to think
It shows the third person that respected peers already lean this way
It proves the argument is correct beyond any question, so no reasons need explaining
It replaces the need to give any reasons at all, since the numbers alone persuade
items.explanation: Peer alignment changes the frame of the conversation, and it works alongside real reasons, not instead of them.

choices: Private conversations are useless, so only what is said in the meeting itself ever counts
The colleague must have been lying throughout the earlier talk
Private agreement helps only if it survives the room, so ask what each ally will say
Dev should have invited every attendee to argue against him
items.explanation: Early conversations build alignment; confirming what an ally will say publicly is part of the work.

choices: Start with the ally, so later conversations can cite real support
Start with the opponent, since winning there makes the rest easy
Talk to both in the same moment, to look balanced and fair to all
Skip the ally, since allies never need any persuading at all
items.explanation: Each conversation makes the next easier when it begins with the most open person.

items.prompt: How many tech leads make a majority of four?
choices: Two, since it is exactly half
Three
Four, since all must agree
items.explanation: A majority is more than half; three of four qualifies.

items.prompt: In the demo, which step produces the biggest jump in odds?
choices: From two allies to three
From zero allies to one ally
From three allies to four allies
items.explanation: The curve jumps when a majority is reached.

items.prompt: Is the odds curve in the demo measured from real data?
choices: Yes, it comes from a survey of many companies
Yes, it comes from a study of company VPs
No, it is an illustrative teaching model
items.explanation: The numbers show the shape of the idea, not a measurement.

items.prompt: What does two of four allies look like?
choices: A guaranteed win
A guaranteed loss
A split room
items.explanation: Without a majority, the outcome is still open.

items.prompt: Why is a majority worth more than its share of allies?
choices: It removes the need to hold the meeting
It changes the room's default to already leaning
It makes the signer leave the room before the vote begins
items.explanation: Crossing the threshold changes what the room expects.

items.prompt: Which line best describes the odds from zero to four allies?
choices: A jump near the majority
A perfectly straight line upward
A line that falls as allies increase
items.explanation: The jump between two and three is the point of the chart.

items.prompt: How many allies does Dev have at the start?
choices: None of the four
Two of the four
All four of them
items.explanation: He begins with no tech lead on his side.

items.prompt: Do the odds reach 100 percent at four allies in the demo?
choices: Yes, they reach exactly 100 percent
No, they fall back to 10 percent
No, they are capped at 92 percent
items.explanation: Even full support leaves some uncertainty in the model.

items.prompt: Dev has two of four tech leads leaning his way, and a third is undecided. According to the threshold idea, how should he read his position?
choices: Nearly won, since half the leads already agree
Lost, since a minority cannot sway the signer
A split room, where the third lead is worth more than the first two suggest
Unchanged, since only unanimity counts
items.explanation: Half is not a majority. The third ally is the one that flips the default, so effort should go there.

items.prompt: What is reciprocity?
choices: Collecting repayment for a favor from long ago
Trading real help now for support later
Asking for help without offering anything back
items.explanation: It is an active two-way exchange.

items.prompt: Which favor builds the most trust?
choices: One offered in the same breath as the ask
One offered unprompted, long before any ask
One announced loudly to the whole team, with a thank-you
items.explanation: Distance from the ask makes it read as genuine.

items.prompt: How big should the favor be compared with the ask?
choices: Always far larger than the ask
Always far smaller than the ask
Roughly the same size
items.explanation: A small favor does not buy a very large ask.

items.prompt: What can a small favor realistically buy?
choices: Fifteen honest minutes to be heard
Public support on a contested decision
Control over the final decision itself
items.explanation: Time to be heard is often the real bottleneck.

items.prompt: Dev reviews Sana's plan a month before raising his concern. What is this?
choices: A performative deposit made for effect
A genuine deposit
A formal approval of her plan
items.explanation: It was unprompted and well ahead of the ask.

items.prompt: Is reciprocity a favor bank where old chips are cashed in?
choices: No, it is an active two-way exchange
Yes, old favors can be cashed in at any time
Yes, but only with one's own manager
items.explanation: Old chips are not the model; ongoing exchange is.

items.prompt: What risk does a performative favor carry?
choices: It always raises trust a little
It has no effect on trust at all, in either direction
It can lower trust if recognized as a setup
items.explanation: Insincere timing is easy to spot.

items.prompt: Why offer help with no ask attached?
choices: It guarantees a yes when you ask later
It lets you skip the later conversation
It shows you help without needing something back
items.explanation: That is what makes the later ask read as fair.

items.prompt: Dev did one small favor for a tech lead last week and now asks her to publicly back his contested proposal. What is the most likely result?
choices: She agrees at once, since any favor creates a debt that must always be repaid in full
The ask outweighs the favor, so she hesitates even though the favor was real
She is offended, since a favor should never be followed by a request of any kind at all
She agrees willingly, since a favor done recently counts for double its original value
items.explanation: Size matters: a small deposit does not cover a large ask.
items.reference:
Genuine deposit

Offered well before any ask, unprompted, for its own sake

Performative deposit

Offered right before the ask, easy to read as a setup

Why: an obviously timed favor can subtract from trust rather than add to it.
items.learnMore:
Reciprocity: genuine, and sized to the ask

Not every favor counts the same, and not every ask is the same size.

items.prompt: What does framing around the listener's stakes mean?

Showing what the position does for them
Using more technical words to explain the underlying risk

What the listener already cares about

Yes, it is always manipulation

items.prompt: What is a credible messenger?

Someone with standing on the topic who carries your point
Someone who reports to the same manager
items.explanation: Their standing makes the point land.

The tech lead for the Payments team

A gap in the asker's own standing

The listeners never read what they get

Someone who has never run a cutover
Someone chosen by drawing lots

Nobody until the decision is made
The few people still unconvinced

Withdraw the concern and say nothing more
